newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait favours China howitzer, British missile.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait favours China howitzer, British missile.

text.p: Kuwait appears to favour a Chinese self-propelled gun and British Sea Skua missiles in deals possibly worth a total $400 million, industry and political sources said on Monday.

"We believe that Kuwait is now in favour of buying one battalion of self-propelled guns from China," said a Western industry source, adding that the requirement had been recently discussed by the country's Supreme Defence Council.
There has been no official statement on decisions by the Defence Council.

The Kuwait Land Forces have a total requirement for three battalions armed with the tracked guns. Industry experts said a deal with China, seen by some as a "political decision" to reward Beijing for its stand during the 1990-91 Gulf crisis, could be worth up to $300 million.

"I think the Council decided on backing the Defence Ministry in its insistence to buy the Sea Skuas," said a Kuwaiti political source of the controversial deal worth around $90 million. "But I have not heard of the Chinese deal".

Industry sources said that Kuwait was in favour of pursuing the Chinese offer which is facing strong competition mainly from the British Desert AS90, the South African LIW 155mm G6 and the American M109 A6 Paladin.
Kuwait has run several mobility and firing tests of the various guns on offer. U.S. forces in Kuwait have the Paladin mounted on fighting vehicles deployed near the border with Iraq.
The government and parliament often clash over arms deals, delaying a $12 billion 1992-2004 arms procurement plan, industry experts said.

"We are not objecting or seeking a fight with the government," MP Nasser al-Sanea, head of parliament's finance committee, told Reuters on Monday. "We just want to make sure that the government follows the right procedure when buying arms and that there are no violations" in spending public funds.
News in late March of government moves to finalise the Sea Skua deal triggered a fresh uproar in parliament although the government had earlier said its decision was final.

Some MPs are insisting that parliament's Public Funds Protection Committee should probe the deal for the British Aerospace Plc surface-to-surface missiles after a cheaper offer for France's Aerospatiale MM-15 was dropped.
The missiles will arm Kuwait's eight French-made fast patrol boats ordered at a cost of $500 million in 1995.
